title: Best Partners
dateline: Selrick Academy. The end of that year.
mood: An empty chair, two small blue badges, a photo taken three times, and a lesson about who sends the Enders.

hero.alt: Comic panel of the ceremony: black-haired Vexana smiles toward their teacher, seen from the side at the left, and pink-haired Guinevere laughs with her eyes shut, both with small blue shield badges pinned below the gold stars at their collars, while other students cheer behind them.
hero.credit: Official Guinevere and Vexana comic, page 25

segs.t: Vexana waited at the side of the hall with her hands folded behind her back.
The patrons had the front row. One chair had a card on it: HOUSE BAROQUE. The chair was empty.
Two rows behind it sat a woman in a gray coat, upright, her hands in her lap. Hester. Vexana remembered her upright in a spinning teacup, a cake box on her knees.
Nobody sat anywhere for Vexana. She had not expected anyone.
Beside her, Guinevere looked at the empty chair. Once. Then she lifted her chin toward the stage and did not look at it again.
She has a door too,
thought Vexana.
She did not ask.
Guinevere stood at the front of the hall with Vexana beside her. Lesley faced them with two badges in her palm.

They were small blue shields with the Academy’s crest. Once a year the instructors would give them to one pair, the best Aspirant Duo of the year. These were the first the Academy had ever given. Every pair in the hall had wanted them.
Lesley pinned one on Guinevere’s chest, below the gold star at her collar, then one on Vexana’s. Her fingers were quick and cool.
“Undefeated,” she said. That was the whole speech.
Guinevere looked down at the blue shield.
She had written to her father a week ago. One line: the day, and what for. No answer had come. She had not asked Hester for one.
Before the summer she had carried a paper with the top mark across the city. She had sat all day on a bench outside his office with it on her knee. By the fountain they had called that score bought.
No more benches,
she thought.
And try buying this one. Half of it is hers.
“Closer, please,” said the camera droid at the foot of the stage.
Vexana reached over without a word. Her gloved fingers found Guinevere’s left bow, which had slipped on the run to the hall, and set it straight.
Guinevere went still.
The bows had been her mother’s. Hester had tied them in her hair the first morning it was long enough. For years now nobody had touched them but Guinevere.
She let Vexana.
Then Vexana’s hand came down and found hers.
At the edge of the stage, Lesley smiled. It was small, and it stayed.
The hall began to cheer. Guinevere squeezed the hand in hers and flung her other arm up.
“We’re the best partners in The Aspirants!”
The camera flashed.
For a moment there was only white. When it cleared, the hall was still cheering. Vexana’s glove was still tight around her fingers.
“Once more,” said the droid. “Someone blinked.”
“Vexana blinked,” said Guinevere.
“I did not.”
The camera flashed again. “Once more.”
Guinevere turned her head. “You said no to me. Twice.”
“I remember.”
“And here we are.” Guinevere bumped her shoulder. “No matter how many times we start over, our fate won’t change.”
The camera flashed. Vexana had turned her head too, and she was smiling. That was the picture they kept.
“Now back to back,” said the droid. “For the courtyard.”

Within the week that one covered the courtyard wall: the two of them back to back, and their names in big letters, GUINEVERE and VEXANA. Under it ran a line about their undefeated record. The first morning it hung there, Guinevere stood under it until the bell.
Before the hall emptied, the droid printed the hand-in-hand picture, one copy each, in a thin black frame.
Vexana held hers flat against her chest.
The crowd poured out through the wide doors, cheering. Guinevere unpinned her badge and held it over her head the whole way out. Somebody whistled. She held it higher.
In Chang’e’s classroom Guinevere took the back row beside Vexana. She had pinned her badge back on in the corridor, crooked. Vexana’s had never come off.
The room had a screen the width of one wall and a tall stool beside it. Layla sat at the front, alone.
The droid had sent the photo to both their phones. Under the desk, Guinevere typed two words and sent them.
BEST PARTNERS.
Vexana’s phone lit on the desk. Behind the words was the photo from the hall. She had made it her wallpaper.
Vexana slid the phone into her pocket. She did not look over.
Guinevere grinned at the back of Layla’s head until her face hurt.
Chang’e climbed onto the stool. Mr. Bunny floated at her shoulder.
“Who sends the Enders?” she asked.
“Nobody knows,” said Layla.
“Somebody does.”

The door opened. A blonde girl from the Science Division slipped in late, on foot. At her heel clicked a machine shaped like a silver dragon, blue light along its seams and an empty seat on its back. She sat by the wall, opened a sketchbook and began to draw. Armor, from what Guinevere could see.

blocks.caption: Late, on foot, with a silver dragon at her heel.

media.alt: In a sunlit Academy corridor a blonde girl in uniform, small red horns in her hair, gives a lazy salute as a silver dragon-shaped machine crackling with blue light swoops past at her side.

segs.t: “We think it is a mind,” Chang’e said. “The Will of the Planet.”
“Whose mind?” Guinevere asked before she could stop herself.

“The planet’s own, maybe. The oldest records give a rule.” Chang’e held up one finger. “When a planet that holds Balance finds a people grown too strong, strong enough to endanger others, it sends the Enders.”
“Balance?” asked a boy in the second row.
“Everything kept in check. Nothing allowed to grow too big.”
Layla’s hand went up. “Endanger who?”
“The records don’t say. And I can’t tell you that rule is what happened here.” Chang’e tapped the screen. “That’s theory. Write it down as theory.”
Guinevere did not write anything. She was thinking of the claw that had raked her arm, in a street at the dome’s foot.
Somebody sent that.
“The Will has a body too, the readings suggest. Something vast, far out where we can’t see,” said Chang’e. “We call that the Mother Matrix.”
By the wall, the blonde girl’s pen did not stop.
“And the Enders?” asked Layla.
“What it sends.”
Chang’e put her finger down. “One thing I’m sure of. To defeat the Will of the Planet, we must destroy the Enders’ Control Core, hidden in its dark void.”
“Their what?” said the same boy.
“Whatever steers them all. That’s what the name means.”
Guinevere sat up.
Something to hit.
Beside her, Vexana’s hand went still on the desk.
“Then we break it,” said Guinevere.
“Good,” said Chang’e. “Where?”
“In the void.”
“Show me the door.”
Guinevere opened her mouth. Nothing came.

“Outside the dome, the Enders come out of portals,” said Chang’e. “Our gate portal only joins one street to another. At the edge of theirs, every reading we have drops to nothing. Whatever lies past that, we call the void.”
“How do you know anything steers them?” asked Layla.

Chang’e pointed at the screen, at a row of jagged lines. “Our screens read a signal off every Ender near the dome. When a lull begins, the weeks they go quiet, every signal stops in the same moment. Something switches them all off at once.”
“So how do we get to the void?” asked Layla.
Guinevere had been about to ask it. Layla always asked first.
“I don’t know yet.” Chang’e said it flat, and Guinevere could see she hated saying it. “Nobody can get near it. I’m working on it.”
The room was very quiet.
“I have one idea, in a paper on black holes.”
“A what?” said the same boy.
“A place in space so heavy it swallows whatever comes too near. Nothing anyone has ever seen fall in has come back out. Not even light.”
“Then what’s the idea?” Guinevere got it out ahead of Layla.
Chang’e folded her hands. “The paper is untested, and I don’t teach untested things. I won’t send a student anywhere I can’t bring them back from.”
Vexana looked up.
She said nothing. Guinevere saw her eyes stay on Chang’e a long moment, the way they stayed on a bent bracket.
Chang’e looked around at the grim faces.
She hopped down off the stool. “The Aspirant power is strong.”
At the back of the room, the light of the screen caught two blue badges.
